title: Why Longevity Research Should Focus on Women
gist: A Buck Institute-led team publishing in Cell proposes the Reproductive Resilience Hypothesis to explain why women outlive men despite more late-life frailty, and why highly fertile females such as queen bees far outlive drones — patterns the standard reproduction-versus-longevity tradeoff cannot account for. Short news item that states the framework but not its mechanism.

themes.theme: The paradoxes the field can’t explain

insights.claim: Women live longer than men yet experience more frailty later in life, a combination that standard aging models treat as anomalous rather than explaining.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Lifespan and healthspan diverge by sex — relevant to how longevity endpoints and trial populations are chosen.
insights.locator: For example, they live longer than men

insights.claim: Extraordinarily fertile females such as queen bees live considerably longer than both non-fertile females and males, with queens living years while drones live only weeks.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: The cleanest natural experiment against the resource-tradeoff model of aging.

insights.claim: A team led by scientists from the Buck Institute for Research on Aging has published a framework in Cell called the Reproductive Resilience Hypothesis to reconcile sex differences in lifespan with fertility.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
entities: Buck Institute for Research on Aging
insights.so_what: Named, citable framework to track — shifts longevity research attention toward female reproductive biology.
insights.locator: A team led by scientists from the Buck Institute

insights.claim: The traditional model treats reproduction and longevity as opposed because resources spent on offspring cannot go to body maintenance, but that logic fails to explain either the female lifespan advantage or the queen bee case.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: If the tradeoff model is wrong, interventions derived from caloric-restriction-style resource logic may be mistargeted.
insights.quote: After all, resources are limited, and those invested in offspring can’t be utilized for regular body maintenance.

insights.claim: Across many species, the females that invest most heavily in offspring are also the ones that live longest, inverting rather than merely weakening the expected reproduction-longevity tradeoff.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Suggests reproductive investment activates protective maintenance pathways — a different therapeutic target set than damage-repair aging.
insights.quote: In fact, in many species, the females that invest more heavily in their offspring also live longer lives.

top_entities: Buck Institute for Research on Aging
